content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued a recommendation regarding the optimal duration of bladder catheterization following the surgical repair of simple obstetric urinary fistula. This guidance is based on evidence and aims to improve the postoperative care and recovery of affected women. An obstetric fistula is an abnormal opening between a woman’s genital tract and her urinary tract and/or rectum, typically caused by prolonged obstructed labor. This condition results from ischemic damage to soft tissues due to compression by the fetal head against the pelvic bones during labor. If the mother survives such labor, she may develop a fistula, leading to continuous leakage of urine and/or feces, which can severely impact her quality of life. Surgical repair is the standard treatment for most obstetric urinary fistulae, particularly vesicovaginal fistulae. Postoperative care typically involves the use of an indwelling urinary catheter to ensure continuous urine drainage and to facilitate tension-free healing of the surgical site. However, the duration of catheterization varies widely in clinical practice, ranging from 5 to 42 days. This variability has significant implications for patient outcomes, healthcare costs, and resource allocation. Prolonged bladder catheterization, while intended to ensure complete healing, can be associated with several drawbacks. These include increased patient discomfort, higher risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infections (UTIs), erosion of the urethra or bladder, and the need for more intensive nursing care. Additionally, longer catheterization periods may necessitate extended hospital stays, particularly in low-income settings where outpatient management is not feasible. This can place a financial and logistical burden on both patients and healthcare systems. Shorter durations of postoperative bladder catheterization, typically between 7 and 10 days, have been studied and shown to be effective in promoting complete healing. This approach may improve patient comfort, reduce the risk of catheter-related complications, and decrease the demand for healthcare resources. The WHO recommends this shorter duration as an alternative to longer catheterization periods for women recovering from the surgical repair of simple obstetric urinary fistula. The WHO defines a simple fistula as a mid-anterior vaginal wall fistula with minimal scarring and a diameter of 3 cm or less. For more complex cases, alternative management strategies may be required. The recommendation is applicable in any context where women experience simple obstetric urinary fistula due to obstructed labor. The evidence supporting this recommendation was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. While the overall quality of evidence was graded as low to moderate, the recommendation takes into account the balance of benefits and harms, stakeholder values and preferences, and resource implications. The WHO acknowledges some uncertainty in the outcomes of shorter versus longer catheterization durations but emphasizes the potential benefits of improved patient comfort, reduced infection risks, and decreased healthcare demands. To ensure proper understanding and implementation of this recommendation, the WHO has provided accompanying remarks and evidence summaries. These materials are intended to guide healthcare professionals, including fistula surgeons and nurses, in delivering effective postoperative care. The guideline is also relevant for policymakers and organizations involved in fistula care services. The WHO plans to regularly review and update this recommendation as new evidence becomes available, with major updates occurring at least every five years. Suggestions for additional questions to address in future updates are welcomed.
